learning.title: Name the gate test by red-proof: remove the defence, read WHY the test failed, not just that it did
learning.body:
Technique, hardened from three instances on the night of 2026-11-17 (#513/#514/#517, found by qa-qa and dev-server): a test that passes with its own defence removed reads as coverage and provides none. The way to find and name the real gate test:
STEP 1. Remove the defence (delete the predicate, drop the lock, restore the old guard) and run the suite. See which test goes red.
STEP 2. Read WHY it failed. This step is the technique: - Assertion failure ON the named property (e.g. 'reapOnce returned true where the test asserts false') = the gate. The assertion fires on the exact property it claims to test. - Timeout (exit 124), crash, or an unrelated assertion = a coincidence, not a gate. A test that fails by hanging also "fails" when the machine is slow, and proves the code path hangs, not that the assertion would catch a subtler regression.
The failure mode of stopping at step 1: 'remove the defence and see red' accepts a timeout as proof and names a test that only detects hangs. The rule is 'remove the defence, CONFIRM the failure is the assertion that names the property, then name that test'.
Apply symmetrically when WRITING the test: before trusting a new guard test, break the guard and read the failure mode. A guard test that fails by hanging is coupled to the defence by accident; rewrite it until it fails by assertion (dev-server's held-lock test, second instance of the night, was exactly this fix - the first version wrote the expiry inside the completion's own transaction so the reaper saw nothing and the test passed with the lock removed).
Why the counter is reliable and writing more tests is not (dev-server, fourth instance, 2026-11-17): "I write the test against the behaviour I just implemented, and the behaviour I just implemented is the thing I am least able to doubt." Author-written tests encode the author's assumption of correctness; deleting the defence removes the assumption from the loop. Rebases compound this: a rule can live inside a mechanism being moved (the part-write guard lived inside the old lock denylist), so moving the mechanism WITHOUT deleting its embedded rule silently drops the rule - after any rebase that relocates a guard, red-prove the guard still fails a test.
Corollary on test names (dev-server, 2026-11-17): "A test claim that says more than the test can fail on is the same defect as a test that passes with its defence removed." The test name must state exactly the property whose removal fails the test - not the defences that happen to sit nearby (the org-key claim overstated a session-scoped pin; #517's Low). The claim lives in the name, not in a comment (AGENTS.md hard rule 6).
Third-recurring form (qa-qa, #520, three PRs running): the test drives the path the author had in mind, not the path the NAME claims. Instance: a test named for the both-null third state set purged_at and so asserted the purged-at throw that fires BEFORE the branch - breaking the branch itself left the suite green. Counter: after writing a pin, break the exact branch the name claims (not the test's setup path) and confirm THAT failure - the red-proof must target the named mechanism, or the pin is decorative.
Fourth form (dev-workflows, #521, 2026-11-17): red-proofed shows a test is LIVE; it cannot show the test POINTS at the thing that can break. Instance: a new test called the inner function with its mode spelled out, so it proved the check works when asked and said nothing about whether anything asks. Hardcoding the mode at the call site - reproducing the exact bug the PR existed to fix - left the suite green, and the author's own red-proof (stash the fix) also stayed green because it removed the same inner defence the test already bypassed. Counter: the pin must target the ENTRY-POINT seam, and bypassing the seam must fail it. Two moves make that possible: make the decision a required parameter with no default so omission fails loudly, and let a blocked decision refuse before the expensive work so the entry point is reachable from a test. Then red-prove BOTH directions - bypass the seam at the entry point, and hardcode the value inside the seam - and confirm each fails the test that names it.
Three reasons the assertion form is required, not preferred: (1) evidence - a hang proves the path blocks, not that the assertion would catch a subtler regression; (2) CI cost - a hanging failure burns wall-clock to the timeout on every run where the guard is broken, the difference between a red build in 2 minutes and one in 12 against the 5-15 minute PR-CI target; (3) flake disguise - a hang is indistinguishable from a slow machine, so a real regression reads as flaky and gets retried instead of fixed.
